title: No doubt in it
hook: a book for the mindful: those who believe in the unseen, pray, and give (2:2–3)
tomorrow: The one who lit a fire

segments.voice: Yesterday: praise, and your line, praise first. The Fatiha ended asking for a path. Today the next page answers.

The Fatiha's last request is show us the straight path. Turn one page. Surah al-Baqarah opens with three Arabic letters, alif, lam, mim, whose meaning, most scholars say, God alone knows. And then, as if answering the request just made, the second verse. In Pickthall's words: “This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil).” You asked for guidance. Here it is. But notice who it says the guidance is for. Today: taqwa.
screen: `SHOW US THE STRAIGHT PATH.` → `ALIF, LAM, MIM.` → `HERE IS THE GUIDANCE.`

segments.voice: Those who ward off evil. Pickthall's phrase translates one Arabic word: al-muttaqin, the people of taqwa. Taqwa comes from a root, w-q-y, meaning to guard, to shield yourself. It gets translated as fear of God, piety, God-consciousness, mindfulness; each catches a piece. A story from the early commentaries, retold by Ibn Kathir, gives a picture. Umar asked the companion Ubayy ibn Ka'b what taqwa is. Ubayy asked him: have you ever walked a path full of thorns? Yes. And what did you do? I gathered up my clothes and watched every step. That, said Ubayy, is taqwa. Not terror. Attention. Verse three says what these mindful people look like: they believe in the unseen, they establish the prayer, and they spend from what they've been given. Trust in what you can't see. A practice that keeps returning, five times a day. And open hands. Here's what stands out: the book says it's guidance for the mindful, not guidance that makes you mindful first and then guides you. Many commentators read it as a loop. A little attention lets you hear the book, and the book deepens the attention. Look back at this week: a whole book opened, seven verses said seventeen times a day, a conversation where every line gets an answer, praise before asking. All of it was about attention. Taqwa is the name for that attention, walking carefully through a thorny world with God in mind.
screen: `AL-MUTTAQIN: THOSE WHO GUARD THEMSELVES` · `WALKING A PATH OF THORNS` · `THE UNSEEN, THE PRAYER, OPEN HANDS` · `THIS WEEK WAS ABOUT ATTENTION`

segments.voice: Pick something small in front of you, a glass of water, standing up, your shoes, and do it slowly, the way you'd walk a path with thorns: the weight of the glass, the cold, the swallow. Then let the attention rest on your breath. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you begin.
Taqwa. Mindfulness of God; from a root meaning to guard yourself, like gathering your clothes on a thorny path. The Qur'an calls itself guidance for the people of taqwa. Today's word.
Your line: guidance for the mindful. A little attention, and the book can be heard. Day three hundred thirty-six, and counting.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of taqwa as the aim of worship itself: the Qur'an names it as the purpose of fasting, and many say bismillah before ordinary acts to bring God to mind as they begin.

chat.says: What does taqwa mean? I've heard it translated as fear of God.
options: Mindfulness of God, like gathering your clothes on a thorny path.
Being so terrified of God that you never feel at peace.
A kind of fasting that's kept only during Ramadan.
